items.originalTitle: Cenk Uygur goes all in on Ro Khanna for 2028
items.author: Will Steakin
items.title: Cenk Uygur goes all in on Ro Khanna for 2028
items.summary: Ro Khanna hasn't launched a 2028 bid yet, but he already has a pioneer of the populist left in his corner. Progressive firebrand Cenk Uygur is set to formally endorse the California Democrat on Thursday night during his annual appearance on nephew Hasan Piker's Twitch stream, a Thanksgiving Day debate-a-thon the pair call "Cenksgiving." Uygur told POLITICO he will pitch Khanna as the best populist progressive candidate. His Rebellion PAC will also debut its first 2028 ad promoting a Khanna candidacy Thursday night. "For me, it's a no-brainer," Uygur said in an interview, explaining why he’s backing Khanna. "Who else would you back, and why would any progressive or any populist back anyone else?" Along with his PAC getting behind Khanna, Uygur is also launching his own "Draft Ro" website to collect signatures and showcase other early high-profile endorsers, though he wouldn't say who just yet. The endorsement is one of the first of the 2028 cycle, and it comes before any major candidate has formally announced. Inside Washington, Khanna’s chances are viewed as quite slim. But for Uygur, that kind of underestimation is exactly part of the draw. "I love it," Uygur said of the skepticism. "I wouldn't have backed him if anyone in D.C. was behind him." "We're running against Washington," he added. "So if Washington doesn't like a candidate, perfect." Uygur is pairing his endorsement with a litmus test he’s trying to lay down for 2028 progressives: Candidates must call what Israel has done in Gaza a genocide and support ending U.S. funding for Israel. "It isn't actually about Israel," Uygur said. "It's about: Is this person going to represent us or not?" Khanna, he said, is "among the very, very few, and maybe the only candidate, that'll pass that test." He allowed for one other: "There's also AOC. If she runs, that's another person that could pass the test." But that's as far as the praise goes. His endorsement of Khanna comes as many other progressives are waiting to see whether Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) jumps in. Uygur isn't one of them. Asked if her entry would change his calculus, he said: "Not 1%." "Sorry, but I don't think AOC means it," he said. "I don't think she would do any of the things that she says, and so I'm not going to back someone who is not going to deliver." "She's obsessed with the establishment, so she's going to run a soft, weak race," he added. "She wants to make Democratic leaders and mainstream media happy. Good luck with that strategy." Khanna has told POLITICO he plans to decide whether to run after the holidays and that whether Ocasio-Cortez gets in won't factor into his decision. Uygur's backing could give the potential 2028 candidate some credibility on the populist left, not to mention a boost from "The Young Turks," one of the longest-running and most popular progressive shows online, which Uygur launched in 2002. He also co-founded Justice Democrats in 2017 and ran a long-shot bid of his own for the 2024 Democratic presidential nomination. His Rebellion PAC sparked controversy during the 2026 midterms with an ad tying U.S. funding for Israel to higher grocery prices, which the campaign of then-Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed distanced itself from. Uygur, who was also a prominent backer of Vermont independent Sen. Bernie Sanders' presidential runs, has a blunt prediction for 2028: "I'm positive Ro Khanna is going to win."

items.originalTitle: CT has built something healthcare can’t afford to waste
items.author: Michelle Puhlick
items.title: CT has built something healthcare can’t afford to waste
items.summary: Connecticut has spent the past several years building the connections needed to make health information sharing a reality across the state. Now comes the more important work: putting that information to use in ways that change lives. As healthcare providers face growing demands to address disparities and do more with limited resources, timely access to reliable health information has never mattered more. Michelle Puhlick " data-large-file="https://ctmirror.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Michelle-Puhlick.png" src="https://ctmirror.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Michelle-Puhlick.png" alt="" class="wp-image-1190314" style="width:169px;height:auto"/> Michelle Puhlick As I step into the role of interim executive director of the Health Information Alliance, Inc. (HIA), I see an opportunity to build on the foundation we’ve established through Connie, Connecticut’s statewide Health Information Exchange, and turn connected data into more informed decisions and better health outcomes. We’ve built the infrastructure. Now, we’re focused on what it can make possible. I’ve been part of Connie’s journey since before it launched in 2021, helping establish the operational foundation and connections for statewide information sharing. This transition is built on years of collaboration and a shared vision for what Connie can become. We’re now entering the phase where that groundwork starts to pay off, as we put the data to work for patients and providers in even more meaningful ways, and I’m committed to carrying that mission forward with energy and focus. Connie now connects more than 4,000 provider locations across Connecticut, helping healthcare providers, payers and public health entities securely share information that supports coordinated, high-quality care. We’ve expanded participation among skilled nursing facilities and pharmacies, connected our first behavioral health electronic medical record systems and brought our first emergency medical services provider onto the network. These milestones give care teams more opportunities to see the bigger picture and make informed decisions. They also reflect our participants’ trust in Connie and Connecticut’s collective commitment to improving care. Additionally, we’re: • Demonstrating Connecticut’s leadership in addressing health information exchange challenges nationwide, with Connie among just nine organizations selected nationally for a pilot grant to advance electronic consent management for patients receiving behavioral health care. • Helping providers improve race, ethnicity and language data, enabling more complete, accurate information to inform efforts to make healthcare more equitable. • Developing tools that give home and community-based services providers access to timely health information to support more coordinated, whole-person care. These accomplishments give us a strong foundation, but I believe our greatest opportunity lies ahead. Our next phase is about putting the information and infrastructure we’ve built to work in more meaningful ways. That means using data to help identify patients who may benefit from earlier intervention, strengthening public health response and supporting more equitable outcomes across Connecticut. It also means continuing to improve data quality and expand the network while ensuring the organizations that depend on Connie can realize its full value. Rural health will be an important focus. Through Connecticut’s Rural Health Transformation Program , we’re working on initiatives to help providers identify rural patients at risk of avoidable hospitalizations and unnecessary emergency department visits. Better information and earlier insights give care teams more opportunities to intervene before a health concern becomes a crisis. We’re pursuing this work in partnership with the providers, state agencies and community organizations that understand Connecticut’s needs firsthand. Technology alone cannot solve the challenges facing healthcare. Progress depends on listening to providers and patients and acting on what they tell us as we build practical solutions together. That includes guidance from our Clinical Advisory Council, Patient and Family Advisory Council and the feedback we gather at community events across the state. My commitment is to carry forward Connie’s mission while continually asking how we can do more with the foundation we’ve established. Our leadership team and staff remain focused on supporting our participants and state partners, and the services and relationships people rely on will continue. What will evolve is how we use our capabilities to create even greater value for the people and communities we serve. I’m proud of what we’ve built so far, but I’m even more energized by what comes next. Connecticut has an opportunity to turn connected health information into more coordinated care and healthier communities. With our partners, we intend to help make that opportunity a reality. Michelle Puhlick is interim executive director and COO of the Health Information Alliance, Inc., the operating entity charged with running Connecticut’s Health Information Exchange, Connie .

items.originalTitle: Is the ‘Connecticut Option’ a good one?
items.author: Dorothy Wilson
items.title: Is the ‘Connecticut Option’ a good one?
items.summary: The Johnson Memorial Hospital campus in Stafford Springs on August 6, 2026. " data-large-file="https://ctmirror.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/TRINITY-QUALITY-0806-JL-012-771x514.jpg" /> Rising health insurance premiums remain a growing concern for Connecticut households. For 2027, average increases of 11.3% and 15.1% have been approved for individual and small-group health insurance plans, respectively. Connecticut needs policies that make health insurance and healthcare services more affordable, especially for people living with chronic diseases. The problem of high healthcare costs in Connecticut is not new. Historically, healthcare costs have gone up faster than household income in Connecticut. A 20-year comparison of average healthcare cost increases and median household income growth shows a 2.8-percentage-point difference: 4.8% compared with 2%. This means healthcare costs increased more than twice as much as household income. Health insurance premiums are rising for several reasons . Medical services and prescription drugs are becoming more expensive, and people are using more healthcare services. Insurance companies are also paying more for medical claims than they expected. Changes in federal financial help for people buying health insurance can also affect premiums. Many Connecticut residents are already struggling with healthcare costs. A 2025 survey of over 1,400 adults found that about 64% had trouble affording healthcare during the previous year. Also, 61% reported delaying or going without healthcare because of cost. So, what does this mean for people living with chronic conditions? Chronic conditions often require ongoing care. People living with diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease, or chronic kidney disease may need regular visits with healthcare providers, lab tests and medicines to manage their conditions and prevent serious health problems. Missing or delaying these services can make their conditions worse and may even put their lives at risk. For these individuals, high insurance premiums add to the financial burden of paying for medicines, frequent visits with healthcare providers, and medical equipment they may need. Moreover, paying for healthcare while also meeting basic needs, such as food, housing, and family expenses, can make life more difficult. Although the Connecticut Insurance Department has made efforts to reduce the yearly premium increases requested by insurance companies, there’s still more to do. The state must put in place policies to ensure that people with chronic conditions can get the medicines, medical equipment, and follow-up care they need without having to pay more than they can afford. Gov. Ned Lamont has proposed the “Connecticut option” as a possible solution to high healthcare costs in the state. This would be a state-designed model managed by private insurance companies. It would include a network of healthcare providers offering quality care at lower costs, which people would be encouraged to use. The Office of Policy and Management has been directed to study whether the plan could work under Public Act 26-68 , and the governor plans to propose legislation in 2027. Organizations such as the Connecticut Hospital Association have raised concerns about the Connecticut option. They worry that the plan could limit patients’ choices of healthcare providers and lead to higher healthcare costs. These concerns are especially important for people living with chronic diseases, who may have regular healthcare providers familiar with their conditions and treatment needs. As the state studies whether the Connecticut Option could work, officials should consider these concerns and work toward a plan that lowers healthcare costs without limiting patients’ access to healthcare providers. Legislators should also consider these concerns when reviewing the proposed plan. Dorothy Wilson is a graduate student at the Elisabeth DeLuca School of Nursing, University of Connecticut.

items.originalTitle: Are Fairfield teenagers getting the mental health care they need?
items.author: Maddie Reed
items.title: Are Fairfield teenagers getting the mental health care they need?
items.summary: here ","orientation":"1"}" data-image-title="child mental health" data-image-description="" data-image-caption="" data-large-file="https://ctmirror.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/child-mental-health-e1795358863171-771x524.jpg" /> Growing up in Fairfield, I saw how much mental health can affect a person, a family, and an entire community. I had multiple friends who struggled with their mental health, and some died by suicide. I have also struggled with my own mental health. These experiences have shown me how important it is for people to feel comfortable asking for help and know where to find it. Fairfield has brought people together to discuss mental health, especially after difficult experiences and losses. These conversations are important, but we also need to make sure teenagers know how to find support. Having resources available is one thing. Knowing how to access them and feeling comfortable using them are different things. Fairfield should make it easier for teenagers to understand their mental health options and access support without feeling embarrassed or unsure where to begin. When I have needed mental-health support, I have struggled to find a therapist in Fairfield who was the right fit, including someone who offered talk therapy or cognitive behavioral therapy. I have ended up looking in nearby towns, including Westport, Norwalk, and New Milford. My experience does not mean Fairfield lacks mental-health providers, but it has made me question how easy it is to find the right support when someone needs it. For teenagers, this process can feel even more overwhelming. They might not know which services are available, how to contact a provider, whether their family can afford treatment, or what information will remain private. Some may fear judgment from friends, while others may not realize they need help. Parents may also struggle to know where to start. When someone is already having a difficult time, figuring out how to get support should not become another challenge. Research supports these concerns. A 2021 review by Jerica Radez and colleagues found that stigma, embarrassment, confidentiality concerns, costs, transportation, and limited knowledge can affect whether young people seek mental-health care. A 2022 study by Alice Villatoro and colleagues also found differences between how adolescents approach mental-health help for themselves and how they recommend it to peers. Encouraging a friend to seek help may feel easier than asking for it personally. Schools can be part of the solution. Research by Mylien Duong and colleagues found that school-based mental-health services were used by about 7% of youth in the general population and about 22% of youth with elevated symptoms or diagnoses. Schools cannot solve every mental-health problem, but they can help students understand what support exists and how to take the next step. Students should not have to search through multiple websites or depend on word of mouth to learn where to turn. Fairfield Public Schools already share social-emotional learning resources, and the town has a Collaborative for Youth Mental Health . These are important starting points. Instead of automatically creating more programs, Fairfield should examine whether teenagers and families can easily find and use the resources already available. Fairfield Public Schools, town officials, families, and local mental-health organizations should work together on three steps. First, they should create one clear, regularly updated guide to local resources, including how to make appointments, available cost and insurance information, and where to ask about confidentiality. Second, schools should regularly discuss mental health in age-appropriate ways and explain how students can seek support. Third, students should have a way to share their concerns anonymously so community leaders can better understand what prevents them from getting help. These efforts should be evaluated over the next school year. Schools could ask students whether they know where to find support before and after these changes. This would help show whether the information is reaching young people instead of assuming that making resources available means students are using them. Listening directly to students would also help Fairfield understand which changes would be most useful. Some may argue that Fairfield already has mental-health resources and community programs. That is a fair point. However, having resources does not automatically mean every teenager knows about them, feels comfortable using them, or can access the right care. Improving access does not mean ignoring what Fairfield already does. It means building on existing efforts and identifying what still gets in the way of young people. Mental health should not become a community conversation only after a tragedy. Teenagers deserve to know where to turn before they reach a crisis point. Fairfield can build on the conversations already happening and make support easier to find and use. Sometimes, helping someone starts with making sure they know help is available and that they do not have to figure everything out alone. Maddie Reed of Fairfield is a fourth-year Human Services major at Elon University interested in youth well-being, mental health, and improving access to support for adolescents.

items.title: Children’s Hospital Throws Thanksgiving Parade for Patients
items.summary: Doctors, nurses and staffers at New York-Presbyterian Morgan Stanley Children’s Hospital got an early start to the Thanksgiving holiday spirit. They threw a special parade complete with floats, balloons and costumes all chosen and designed by patients themselves. TODAY’s Laura Jarrett shares the Morning Boost.
